texts.0: SP, due to late recognition of the DME trend and the use of one large heading change instead of small increments, did not maintain the arc within the published tolerance. Arc distance opened to 3.0 NM and then closed through the nominal value to 0.8 NM, exceeding the +/-2 NM limit in both directions. The IP had to direct the intercept heading to re-establish the arc.
texts.1: SP, due to a delayed response to the increasing DME and reliance on a single oversized correction, allowed arc distance to reach 2.0 NM, at the +/-2 NM limit. The deviation was arrested only after the IP's verbal prompt to turn toward the station, and the arc was re-established slowly and with a further overshoot inbound.
texts.2: SP, due to a late start of the correction turn and an undersized heading change, allowed arc distance to reach 1.5 NM, between the +/-1 NM and +/-2 NM values. SP recognized the trend without prompting and returned inside 1 NM with a timely 20 degree correction, and no IP input was required.
texts.3: SP maintained the arc within +/-1 NM throughout, working the DME with 10 to 20 degree heading increments and correcting each trend as soon as it appeared. Corrections were promptly applied and correctly sized, so the arc distance stabilized without overshoot.
texts.4: SP held arc distance within a few tenths of a mile of the nominal DME for the whole arc. Trends were anticipated from the bearing pointer and neutralized by small heading increments before any measurable deviation developed.
texts.marginal: SP kept arc distance inside the published tolerance but consistently worked the outer part of the band, starting corrections after the DME had already moved rather than on the trend. The result remains within standards, but SP is expected to tighten the arc by anticipating the trend and using smaller, more frequent heading increments.

texts_at.0: SP worked the arc with the IP flying the first correction turns and talking through the DME trend as the exercise began. This is SP's first exposure to arc distance control, and following the DME as a continuous trend rather than a static reading has not yet become a habit. The Training Section introduces this maneuver at this point and does not yet ask for an independent standard. SP is expected to begin following the DME trend independently, with the IP available to confirm the picture.
texts_at.1: SP worked the arc to the standard expected at this stage, letting arc distance drift out to 2 DME, at the tolerance limit, before turning back toward the station. The correction followed the IP's verbal prompt rather than SP's own read of the DME. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to follow the DME trend continuously rather than checking it only once the deviation is already established.
texts_at.2: SP recognized the trend without prompting, letting arc distance drift to about 1.5 DME before turning back toward the station with a timely 20 degree correction. The correction is still triggered once the distance has moved noticeably rather than at the first sign of the trend. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to begin the correction as soon as the DME first shows a trend rather than waiting for it to build.
texts_at.3: SP maintained the arc within 1 DME through most of the arc, working the DME with 10 to 20 degree heading increments and correcting each trend as soon as it appeared. One correction was applied slightly later than the others, without the arc distance leaving the standard. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus. SP is expected to make that correction as promptly as the rest of the arc.

texts_above.1: SP worked the arc, letting arc distance reach about 2.0 NM, at the +/-2 NM limit, before turning back toward the station. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. This is above the level the Training Section requires at this point.
texts_above.2: SP recognized the trend without prompting, letting arc distance reach 1.5 NM before returning inside 1 NM with a timely 20 degree correction. Beginning the correction as soon as the DME first shows a trend, rather than once it has moved noticeably, would keep that peak smaller. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to sound arc-tracking technique.
texts_above.3: SP maintained the arc within +/-1 NM throughout, working the DME with 10 to 20 degree heading increments and correcting each trend as soon as it appeared, with corrections promptly applied and correctly sized so the arc distance stabilized without overshoot. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to very good trend anticipation.
texts_above.4: SP held arc distance within a few tenths of a mile of the nominal DME for the whole arc, anticipating trends from the bearing pointer and neutralizing them with small heading increments before any measurable deviation developed. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to outstanding arc-distance control.

error_modes.label: ALTITUDE CONTROL WHILE WORKING THE ARC

texts.0: SP, due to an attention bottleneck on the DME readout at the expense of the instrument cross-check, did not maintain altitude within the Basic A/C Control tolerance while flying the arc. Altitude decayed 400 feet below the cleared level and was still descending when the IP directed the recovery and took the altitude call. Pitch and power were not reset until the IP intervened.
texts.1: SP, due to absorption in the DME and bearing pointer while the altimeter went unmonitored, allowed altitude to reach 300 feet below the cleared level, at the +/-300 feet limit. The trend was reversed only after the IP called the altitude, and the return to level flight was slow and accompanied by an airspeed excursion.
texts.2: SP, due to a scan that dwelt on the navigation display during each correction turn, allowed altitude to deviate 200 feet, between the +/-150 feet and +/-300 feet values. SP detected the deviation on the following scan and returned inside 150 feet with a smooth pitch and power correction, without any IP input.
texts.3: SP maintained altitude within +/-150 feet throughout the arc, keeping the altimeter and VSI in the scan while working the DME. Small pitch and power corrections were applied early, so level flight was preserved through every heading change.
texts.4: SP held altitude within about 50 feet of the cleared level for the entire arc. The cross-check remained evenly distributed between the navigation display and the primary flight instruments, and no pitch excursion developed during the correction turns.
texts.marginal: SP remained within the altitude tolerance but showed a repeating pattern of a slow altitude drift during each correction turn, followed by a late recovery. Performance is acceptable, but SP is expected to keep the altimeter in the scan through the turns so the deviation does not build before it is caught.

texts_at.0: SP flew the arc with the IP calling the altitude trend and talking through keeping the altimeter in the scan while the DME was worked. This is SP's first exposure to dividing attention between the DME and the flight instruments, and keeping the altimeter in the scan through a correction turn has not yet been built. This is the level of assistance the Training Section still provides at this stage. SP is expected to begin keeping the altimeter in the scan independently through each correction, with the IP available to call any trend that is missed.
texts_at.1: SP held altitude while working the arc to the standard expected at this stage, letting the deviation reach 300 feet below the cleared level before the trend was reversed. The reversal followed the IP calling the altitude rather than SP's own scan. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to keep the altimeter in the scan through each correction turn rather than letting it dwell on the navigation display.
texts_at.2: SP detected the deviation on the following scan without prompting, letting altitude deviate 200 feet before returning to the cleared level with a smooth correction. The scan is still dwelling on the navigation display for a period before the altimeter is brought back in. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to keep the altimeter and the navigation display in the scan together rather than one after the other.
texts_at.3: SP maintained altitude within +/-150 feet throughout the arc, keeping the altimeter and VSI in the scan while working the DME, on most of the arc. One correction turn showed a slightly larger excursion during a busy segment, without the altitude leaving the standard. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus. SP is expected to hold the same scan width through that busy segment as through the rest of the arc.

texts_above.1: SP held altitude while working the arc, letting the deviation reach about 300 feet below the cleared level, at the tolerance limit, before the trend was reversed. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. The result is above the code required for this Training Section at this stage of training.
texts_above.2: SP detected the deviation on the following scan without prompting, letting altitude deviate 200 feet before returning inside 150 feet with a smooth pitch and power correction. Keeping the altimeter and the navigation display in the scan together, rather than one after the other, would keep that deviation smaller. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to solid altitude discipline.
texts_above.3: SP maintained altitude within +/-150 feet throughout the arc, keeping the altimeter and VSI in the scan while working the DME, with small pitch and power corrections applied early so level flight was preserved through every heading change. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to sure-handed scan integration.
texts_above.4: SP held altitude within about 50 feet of the cleared level for the entire arc, with the cross-check remaining evenly distributed between the navigation display and the primary flight instruments so no pitch excursion developed during the correction turns. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to excellent scan distribution.

error_modes.label: AIRSPEED AND POWER MANAGEMENT ON THE ARC

texts.0: SP, due to power settings that were not adjusted for the bank changes required by the arc, did not maintain airspeed within the Basic A/C Control tolerance. Airspeed decayed 25 KIAS below the briefed value, beyond the +/-20 KIAS limit, and the IP had to direct the power increase before the trend was reversed.
texts.1: SP, due to a single late power correction applied after the airspeed had already moved, allowed airspeed to reach 20 KIAS from the briefed value, at the +/-20 KIAS limit. The correction followed the IP's verbal prompt, and the subsequent power change overshot in the opposite direction before airspeed settled.
texts.2: SP, due to a delayed power adjustment during the correction turns, allowed airspeed to deviate 15 KIAS, between the +/-10 KIAS and +/-20 KIAS values. SP identified the trend without prompting and restored the briefed airspeed with a timely power correction and no IP input.
texts.3: SP maintained airspeed within +/-10 KIAS for the whole arc, setting power for the phase of flight and adjusting it as bank was applied and removed. Airspeed remained stable through every heading increment and no large power changes were needed.
texts.4: SP held airspeed within a few knots of the briefed value throughout the arc. Power was anticipated for each turn rather than applied in response to an indication, so the airspeed trace remained essentially flat.
texts.marginal: SP stayed within the airspeed tolerance but let airspeed drift low in each turn and then recovered it with a larger than necessary power change. The result is acceptable, but SP is expected to anticipate the power requirement of the turn so airspeed is held without repeated corrections.

texts_at.0: SP flew the arc with the IP calling the airspeed trend and talking through the power adjustment needed for each bank change. This is SP's first exposure to adjusting power for the bank changes an arc requires, and making that adjustment with the turn has not yet become routine. The maneuver is being introduced at this point of the syllabus, so no independent standard is required yet. SP is expected to begin adjusting power independently with each bank change, with the IP available to call any trend that develops.
texts_at.1: SP held airspeed on the arc to the standard expected at this stage, letting airspeed reach 20 KIAS from the briefed value before the power correction followed the IP's verbal prompt. The overshoot in the opposite direction is still occurring before airspeed settles. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to make a single measured power correction rather than one that has to be followed by a second, opposite one.
texts_at.2: SP identified the trend without prompting, letting airspeed deviate 15 KIAS before restoring the briefed airspeed with a timely power correction. The power adjustment during the correction turns is still made a moment after the turn is started rather than with it. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to adjust power together with the turn rather than after the airspeed has begun to move.
texts_at.3: SP maintained airspeed within +/-10 KIAS for most of the arc, setting power for the phase of flight and adjusting it as bank was applied and removed. One correction was slightly larger following a steeper bank angle, without leaving the standard. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus. SP is expected to keep that correction as fine as the others.

texts_above.1: SP held airspeed on the arc, letting airspeed reach about 20 KIAS from the briefed value, at the tolerance limit, before the power correction was applied. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus.
texts_above.2: SP identified the trend without prompting, letting airspeed deviate 15 KIAS before restoring the briefed airspeed with a timely power correction. Adjusting power together with the turn, rather than after the airspeed has begun to move, would keep that deviation smaller. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to steady power management.
texts_above.3: SP maintained airspeed within +/-10 KIAS for the whole arc, setting power for the phase of flight and adjusting it as bank was applied and removed, with airspeed remaining stable through every heading increment. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to well-developed power anticipation.
texts_above.4: SP held airspeed within a few knots of the briefed value throughout the arc, anticipating power for each turn rather than applying it in response to an indication, so the airspeed trace remained essentially flat. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to superior power anticipation.

texts.0: SP, due to the use of unmeasured turns instead of defined heading increments, did not hold the computed arc heading within the Basic A/C Control tolerance. Heading wandered more than 15 degrees from the required value between corrections, exceeding the +/-10 degrees limit, and the IP had to state the heading to fly to stop the wander.
texts.1: SP, due to rolling out without reference to a target heading, allowed heading to deviate 10 degrees from the computed value, at the +/-10 degrees limit. The correct heading was regained only after the IP prompted the roll-out reference, and the following increment was again flown without a defined target.
texts.2: SP, due to imprecise roll-out from the correction turns, allowed heading to deviate 8 degrees from the computed value, between the +/-5 degrees and +/-10 degrees values. SP recognized the error on the HSI and re-established the required heading promptly, without IP input.
texts.3: SP flew the arc in defined heading increments and held each computed heading within +/-5 degrees. Roll-in and roll-out were accurate and bank was kept appropriate for the turn required, so the arc geometry was preserved.
texts.4: SP held each computed arc heading within about 2 degrees, rolling out precisely on the target value at every increment. Bank angle was selected to match the turn required and no heading chasing was observed.
texts.marginal: SP remained within the heading tolerance but rolled out consistently short of the computed value and then made a second small correction. Performance is acceptable, but SP is expected to select a target heading before each increment and roll out on it in one turn.

texts_at.0: SP flew heading increments on the arc with the IP setting the target heading and talking through the roll-out reference for each turn. This is SP's first exposure to flying the arc in defined heading increments, and selecting a target heading before each one has not yet been built. Performance is consistent with a first exposure at this point of the syllabus, where the Training Section still provides assistance. SP is expected to begin selecting a target heading independently before each increment, with the IP available to confirm the roll-out.
texts_at.1: SP flew heading increments on the arc to the standard expected at this stage, letting heading deviate 10 degrees from the computed value before the IP prompted the roll-out reference. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to select a target heading before each increment rather than rolling out without one.
texts_at.2: SP recognized the error on the HSI without prompting, letting heading deviate 8 degrees from the computed value before re-establishing the required heading promptly. The roll-out from the correction turns is still slightly imprecise rather than exact. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to roll out precisely on the computed heading rather than needing a follow-up correction.
texts_at.3: SP flew the arc in defined heading increments and held each computed heading within +/-5 degrees on most increments, with roll-in and roll-out accurate and bank kept appropriate for the turn required. One increment finished slightly short of the computed value and needed a second small correction, without leaving the standard. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus. SP is expected to roll out on that increment as accurately as on the others.

texts_above.1: SP flew heading increments on the arc, letting heading deviate about 10 degrees from the computed value, at the tolerance limit, before the roll-out reference was confirmed. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage of training.
texts_above.2: SP recognized the error on the HSI without prompting, letting heading deviate 8 degrees from the computed value before re-establishing the required heading promptly. Rolling out precisely on the computed heading, rather than needing a follow-up correction, would remove that deviation. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to dependable heading discipline.
texts_above.3: SP flew the arc in defined heading increments and held each computed heading within +/-5 degrees, with roll-in and roll-out accurate and bank kept appropriate for the turn required so the arc geometry was preserved. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to notably good turn-increment discipline.
texts_above.4: SP held each computed arc heading within about 2 degrees, rolling out precisely on the target value at every increment, with bank angle selected to match the turn required and no heading chasing observed. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to exceptional heading precision.

error_modes.label: NAVIGATION AID SELECTION AND INTERPRETATION (VOR/TACAN/GPS OBS)
error_modes.source: general:a (Basic A/C Control Criteria apply, key d - use of radio aids)

texts.0: SP, due to mode confusion over which navigation source was driving the display, flew the arc against a GPS OBS reference that was not the intended aid and did not identify the station in use. The resulting arc distance exceeded +/-2 NM and the error was resolved only when the IP directed the correct selection and re-identification.
texts.1: SP, due to an incorrect assumption about the active navigation mode, worked the arc from an unverified source and allowed arc distance to reach 2.0 NM, at the +/-2 NM limit. The mis-selection was recognized only after the IP prompted a check of the navigation source, and re-establishment of the arc was delayed.
texts.2: SP, due to selecting the arc reference before confirming the mode of the navigation display, briefly worked from the wrong indication and allowed arc distance to reach 1.5 NM, between the +/-1 NM and +/-2 NM values. SP detected the discrepancy by cross-checking the second source, reselected correctly and closed the arc without IP input.
texts.3: SP selected, identified and cross-checked the VOR/TACAN and the GPS OBS reference before commencing the arc, and remained oriented on the correct source throughout. Arc distance was held within +/-1 NM and the indications of both aids were compared during the turn.
texts.4: SP pre-set and verified both navigation sources, stated the active mode, and continuously compared the two indications while flying the arc. Orientation to the station was maintained at all times and the arc showed no measurable error attributable to the navigation setup.
texts.marginal: SP used the correct navigation source but verified the active mode only once, at the start, and did not re-cross-check it during the arc. The setup was adequate on this sortie, but SP is expected to build in a periodic comparison of the two aids so a mode change would be detected before it affects the arc.

texts_at.0: SP worked the arc with the IP confirming the active navigation source and talking through the identification and cross-check of the aid in use. This is SP's first exposure to verifying which navigation mode is driving the display, and confirming it before working the arc has not yet become a fixed habit. The Training Section still expects IP assistance for this maneuver at this point. SP is expected to begin confirming the active navigation source independently before working the arc, with the IP available to confirm the selection.
texts_at.1: SP used the navigation source on the arc to the standard expected at this stage, letting arc distance reach 2 DME, at the tolerance limit, before the mis-selection was found. The correction followed the IP prompting a check of the source rather than SP's own verification. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to confirm the active navigation mode before working the arc from it, not after a deviation has appeared.
texts_at.2: SP detected the discrepancy by cross-checking the second source without prompting, letting arc distance drift to about 1.5 DME before reselecting correctly and closing the arc. The mode is still confirmed only once, before commencing the arc, rather than periodically through it. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to build in a periodic comparison of the two aids so a mode change is caught sooner.
texts_at.3: SP selected, identified and cross-checked the VOR/TACAN and the GPS OBS reference before commencing the arc, remaining oriented on the correct source throughout most of it, with arc distance held within 1 DME. One stretch of the arc went a little longer than usual between comparisons, without a deviation resulting. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus. SP is expected to keep that comparison interval as short there as elsewhere on the arc.

texts_above.1: SP used the navigation source on the arc, letting arc distance reach about 2.0 NM, at the +/-2 NM limit, before the mis-selection was found and corrected. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. This is above the level the Training Section requires at this point.
texts_above.2: SP detected the discrepancy by cross-checking the second source without prompting, letting arc distance reach 1.5 NM before reselecting correctly and closing the arc. Building in a periodic comparison of the two aids, rather than confirming the mode only once, would catch a mode change sooner. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to assured mode verification.
texts_above.3: SP selected, identified and cross-checked the VOR/TACAN and the GPS OBS reference before commencing the arc and remained oriented on the correct source throughout, with the indications of both aids compared during the turn and arc distance held within +/-1 NM. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to well-developed cross-check habit.
texts_above.4: SP pre-set and verified both navigation sources, stated the active mode, and continuously compared the two indications while flying the arc, maintaining orientation to the station at all times with no measurable error attributable to the navigation setup. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to exemplary navigation discipline.

error_modes.label: WIND DRIFT COMPENSATION AROUND THE ARC
error_modes.source: general:a (Basic A/C Control Criteria apply); conditions:course intercepts

texts.0: SP, due to no allowance for the known wind while transiting the downwind portion of the arc, did not apply a drift correction and let the aircraft be carried away from the station. Arc distance opened to 3.0 NM, beyond the +/-2 NM limit, and the IP had to direct a cut toward the station to recover the arc.
texts.1: SP, due to applying the same heading increment regardless of the wind quadrant, allowed the drift to build until arc distance reached 2.0 NM, at the +/-2 NM limit. The wind effect was addressed only after the IP pointed out the direction of the trend, and the correction was then oversized.
texts.2: SP, due to a drift correction that was recognized late in the downwind sector, allowed arc distance to reach 1.5 NM, between the +/-1 NM and +/-2 NM values. SP identified the wind trend from the repeated DME movement, increased the correction toward the station and re-established the arc without IP assistance.
texts.3: SP applied a wind correction appropriate to each sector of the arc, varying the heading increments so the DME trend was neutralized before it developed. Arc distance was held within +/-1 NM around the full arc, including the downwind portion.
texts.4: SP anticipated the wind effect for every sector of the arc and adjusted the correction continuously, so the DME remained essentially constant. No sector of the arc showed a distance trend attributable to drift.
texts.marginal: SP compensated for the wind but only after the DME had begun to move in each sector, so the correction was always reactive. The arc remained within standards, and SP is expected to pre-plan the drift correction by sector so the deviation is prevented rather than corrected.

texts_at.0: SP flew the arc with the IP setting the drift correction needed for each sector and talking through the DME trend as the wind quadrant changed. This is SP's first exposure to varying the wind correction sector by sector around an arc, and recognizing the repeating DME trend that calls for it has not yet been built. The Training Section introduces this maneuver at this point and does not yet ask for an independent standard. SP is expected to begin recognizing the DME trend independently as the cue for a wind correction, with the IP available to confirm the amount.
texts_at.1: SP compensated for wind around the arc to the standard expected at this stage, letting arc distance drift out to 2 DME, at the outer edge of the standard, before the wind effect was addressed. The correction followed the IP pointing out the direction of the trend rather than SP's own recognition. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to vary the heading increment with the wind quadrant rather than applying the same increment regardless of it.
texts_at.2: SP identified the wind trend from the repeated DME movement without prompting, letting arc distance drift to about 1.5 DME before increasing the correction toward the station. The drift correction is still recognized late in the downwind sector rather than anticipated before it. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to anticipate the downwind sector rather than waiting for the drift to build in it.
texts_at.3: SP applied a wind correction appropriate to each sector of the arc, varying the heading increments so the DME trend was neutralized before it developed, on most of the arc, holding distance within 1 DME including the downwind portion. One sector needed a slightly larger correction, without leaving the standard. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus. SP is expected to size that correction as precisely as in the other sectors.

texts_above.1: SP compensated for wind around the arc, letting arc distance reach about 2.0 NM, at the +/-2 NM limit, before the wind effect was addressed. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. The result is above the code required for this Training Section at this stage of training.
texts_above.2: SP identified the wind trend from the repeated DME movement without prompting, letting arc distance reach 1.5 NM before increasing the correction toward the station. Anticipating the downwind sector, rather than waiting for the drift to build in it, would remove that growth. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to steady wind-drift recognition.
texts_above.3: SP applied a wind correction appropriate to each sector of the arc, varying the heading increments so the DME trend was neutralized before it developed, holding distance within +/-1 NM around the full arc including the downwind portion. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to consistently accurate drift compensation.
texts_above.4: SP anticipated the wind effect for every sector of the arc and adjusted the correction continuously, so the DME remained essentially constant with no sector showing a distance trend attributable to drift. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to first-rate wind anticipation.

error_modes.label: TRIM AND SMOOTHNESS OF CONTROL INPUTS
error_modes.source: general:a (Basic A/C Control Criteria apply, keys a and c)

texts.0: SP, due to flying the arc out of trim and countering the resulting control forces with abrupt inputs, did not handle the aircraft with the required comfort and ease. The uncommanded pitch changes produced altitude excursions beyond +/-300 feet together with an arc error beyond +/-2 NM, and the IP had to take the aircraft to re-trim and stabilize it.
texts.1: SP, due to leaving the aircraft out of trim through the correction turns, flew with continuous control pressures and allowed altitude to reach 300 feet from the cleared level, at the +/-300 feet limit. Trim was reset only after the IP prompted it, and the aircraft remained unsettled for the rest of that arc segment.
texts.2: SP, due to trimming late after each power and bank change, applied larger control inputs than required and allowed altitude to deviate 200 feet, between the +/-150 feet and +/-300 feet values. SP recognized the residual control pressure, re-trimmed and returned the aircraft to a stable condition without IP input.
texts.3: SP kept the aircraft in trim through the power and bank changes of the arc and used smooth, correctly sized control inputs. Altitude stayed within +/-150 feet and arc distance within +/-1 NM, with the aircraft handled with comfort and ease throughout.
texts.4: SP trimmed continuously and flew the arc with minimal control pressures, so heading increments produced no secondary pitch or airspeed disturbance. Aircraft handling was smooth and precise for the whole arc.
texts.marginal: SP kept the aircraft controlled within standards but trimmed only after the deviation appeared, so residual control pressures were carried through the turns. The result is acceptable, and SP is expected to trim immediately after each power and bank change so the aircraft holds the condition without continuous input.

texts_at.0: SP flew the arc with the IP calling the out-of-trim condition and talking through the retrim needed after each power and bank change. This is SP's first exposure to trimming through the power and bank changes an arc requires, and the habit of retrimming rather than holding pressure has not yet been built. This is the level of assistance the Training Section still provides at this stage. SP is expected to begin retrimming independently after each power and bank change, with the IP available to call any residual pressure.
texts_at.1: SP handled the aircraft on the arc to the standard expected at this stage, letting altitude reach 300 feet from the cleared level and arc distance open to 2 DME, both at the tolerance limit, before the trim was reset. The reset followed the IP's prompt rather than SP's own recognition of the out-of-trim condition. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to retrim immediately after each power and bank change rather than flying with continuous control pressure until it is called.
texts_at.2: SP recognized the residual control pressure without prompting, letting altitude deviate 200 feet and arc distance drift to about 1.5 DME before retrimming and returning the aircraft to a stable condition. The trim is still set a moment after the power and bank change rather than with it. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to trim as the power or bank change is made rather than after the residual pressure is felt.
texts_at.3: SP kept the aircraft in trim through the power and bank changes of the arc and used smooth, correctly sized control inputs on most of the arc, with altitude within 150 feet and arc distance within 1 DME. One segment needed a slightly larger control input following a closely spaced pair of corrections, without leaving the standard. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus. SP is expected to keep the same smoothness through that segment as through the rest of the arc.

texts_above.1: SP handled the aircraft on the arc, letting altitude reach about 300 feet from the cleared level, at the tolerance limit, before the trim was reset. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus.
texts_above.2: SP recognized the residual control pressure without prompting, letting altitude deviate 200 feet before retrimming and returning the aircraft to a stable condition. Trimming as the power or bank change is made, rather than after the residual pressure is felt, would keep that deviation smaller. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to dependable trim discipline.
texts_above.3: SP kept the aircraft in trim through the power and bank changes of the arc and used smooth, correctly sized control inputs, with altitude staying within +/-150 feet and arc distance within +/-1 NM, the aircraft handled with comfort and ease throughout. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to notably good handling smoothness.
texts_above.4: SP trimmed continuously and flew the arc with minimal control pressures, so heading increments produced no secondary pitch or airspeed disturbance and aircraft handling was smooth and precise for the whole arc. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to faultless trim management.

texts.0: SP, due to an interrupted instrument cross-check while attention remained on the navigation display, did not monitor the aircraft state and let more than one parameter deviate at the same time. Arc distance exceeded +/-2 NM while altitude exceeded +/-300 feet, and neither trend was identified until the IP intervened and directed the corrections.
texts.1: SP, due to a fixed scan that concentrated on the DME and bearing pointer, missed the developing trends until they reached the code 1 values, with arc distance at 2.0 NM and heading at 10 degrees from the computed value. Both were addressed only after the IP called the deviations, and the scan was not re-established until later in the arc.
texts.2: SP, due to a cross-check that slowed during each correction turn, allowed arc distance to reach 1.5 NM and altitude 200 feet, between the code 3 and code 1 values. SP re-established the scan without prompting, prioritized the deviations correctly and returned both parameters inside the code 3 values without IP input.
texts.3: SP maintained an active cross-check between the navigation display and the primary flight instruments throughout the arc, so trends were caught early. Arc distance stayed within +/-1 NM and altitude, airspeed and heading remained within the Basic A/C Control code 3 values.
texts.4: SP kept a fully distributed cross-check for the entire arc, monitoring the aircraft state continuously while working the navigation solution. Deviations were identified at the moment they began and no parameter was allowed to develop a measurable trend.
texts.marginal: SP kept an adequate cross-check but let it narrow toward the navigation display during each correction turn, catching the flight instruments only after the turn was complete. Performance remains within standards, and SP is expected to keep the primary flight instruments in the scan throughout the turn so no parameter goes unmonitored.

error_modes.label: LEAD POINT NOT REDUCED FOR TURNS OF LESS THAN 90 DEGREES

texts.0: SP, due to applying the full lead point computed for a 90 degree turn at 30 degree bank to a 45 degree turn, did not reduce it to one third as the technique requires. The turn was started far too early and the aircraft rolled out 3.0 NM inside the arc, beyond the +/-2 NM limit, with the DME still decreasing. The IP had to direct the recovery heading to re-establish the arc distance.
texts.1: SP, due to using the uncorrected 90 degree lead point for a 60 degree turn instead of one half of it, turned early and let the arc error reach 2.0 NM, at the +/-2 NM limit. Only after the IP's verbal prompt to stop the turn and take an outbound heading did the DME move back toward the nominal value, and the arc was regained slowly.
texts.2: SP, due to only a partial reduction of the calculated lead point for a turn of less than 90 degrees, rolled out short of the arc and allowed the distance to reach 1.5 NM, between the +/-1 NM and +/-2 NM values. SP recognized the error from the DME trend without prompting and closed back inside 1 NM with a timely correction turn.
texts.3: SP reduced the calculated lead point according to the amount of turn, using one half for 60 degrees and one third for 45 degrees, and rolled out on the arc within +/-1 NM. The DME settled at the nominal value with only a small heading adjustment after roll-out.
texts.4: SP applied the lead point reduction for the actual amount of turn precisely, so the roll-out finished within a few tenths of a mile of the nominal DME. No corrective turn was required afterwards and the arc distance held from the first moment on the arc.
texts.marginal: SP reduced the lead point for the smaller turn but consistently used slightly more lead than the technique gives, so every roll-out finished just inside the arc and on the outer part of the tolerance. The result meets standards, but SP is expected to apply the one half, one third and one sixth reductions as computed so the roll-out lands on the nominal DME.

texts_at.0: SP turned onto the arc with the IP talking through the reduction of the lead point needed for a turn smaller than the full amount. This is SP's first exposure to reducing a computed lead point by fractions of the turn actually flown, and applying the correct fraction has not yet been built. Performance is consistent with a first exposure at this point of the syllabus, where the Training Section still provides assistance. SP is expected to begin reducing the lead point independently by the standard fractions, with the IP available to confirm the amount.
texts_at.1: SP reduced the lead point for smaller turns to the standard expected at this stage, letting the arc error reach 2 DME, at the tolerance limit, before turning back. The correction followed the IP's verbal prompt to stop the turn rather than SP's own reduction of the lead. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to apply the standard one-half or one-third reduction before the turn, not after the roll-out shows the arc has been missed.
texts_at.2: SP recognized the trend on the DME without prompting, letting the arc error grow to about 1.5 DME before closing back inside the desired tolerance with a timely correction turn. The reduction of the lead point is still only partial for the smaller turn. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to apply the full one-half or one-third reduction rather than a partial one.
texts_at.3: SP reduced the calculated lead point according to the amount of turn, using one half for 60 degrees and one third for 45 degrees, and rolled out on the arc within 1 DME on most turns. One turn needed a small heading adjustment after roll-out following a slightly optimistic reduction, without leaving the standard. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus. SP is expected to apply that fraction as precisely on the smaller turns as on the larger ones.

texts_above.1: SP reduced the lead point for the smaller turn, letting the arc error reach about 2.0 NM, at the +/-2 NM limit, before turning back. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. This is above the level the Training Section requires at this point.
texts_above.2: SP recognized the error from the DME trend without prompting, letting the distance reach 1.5 NM before closing back inside 1 NM with a timely correction turn. Applying the full one-half or one-third reduction, rather than a partial one, would remove that excursion. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to steady lead-point reduction.
texts_above.3: SP reduced the calculated lead point according to the amount of turn, using one half for 60 degrees and one third for 45 degrees, and rolled out on the arc within +/-1 NM, with the DME settling at the nominal value with only a small heading adjustment after roll-out. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to well-developed fractional reduction.
texts_above.4: SP applied the lead point reduction for the actual amount of turn precisely, so the roll-out finished within a few tenths of a mile of the nominal DME with no corrective turn required afterwards. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to superior lead-point accuracy.

error_modes.label: TURN RADIUS COMPUTED FROM THE WRONG GROUNDSPEED

texts.0: SP, due to computing the turn radius from indicated airspeed instead of groundspeed in NM per minute, produced a lead point that did not match the actual turn. With the wind component ignored in the NM per minute minus 2 rule, the roll-out finished 2.6 NM outside the arc, past the +/-2 NM limit, and the DME was still opening. The IP had to assign the intercept heading before the trend reversed.
texts.1: SP, due to a turn radius derived from a stale groundspeed rather than the current value, used a lead point about a mile short and let the arc error reach 2.0 NM, at the +/-2 NM limit. The correction was started only after the IP prompted a check of the DME, and the arc was re-established with a further wander.
texts.2: SP, due to a rounding error in the groundspeed to NM per minute conversion before applying the minus 2 rule, rolled out with 1.5 NM of arc error, between the +/-1 NM and +/-2 NM values. SP rechecked groundspeed without prompting, recomputed the radius and closed back inside 1 NM without IP input.
texts.3: SP computed the turn radius from the current groundspeed in NM per minute and used it as the lead point, rolling out on the arc within +/-1 NM. The computed value was cross-checked against the DME behaviour during the turn, so no sizeable correction was needed.
texts.4: SP converted groundspeed to NM per minute and derived the no-wind turn radius accurately with the squared over ten method, placing the roll-out within a few tenths of a mile of the arc. The computed lead point matched the observed DME movement throughout the turn.
texts.marginal: SP used the turn radius formula correctly but worked from a groundspeed figure that was not refreshed as the wind component changed, so the roll-out repeatedly settled on the outer side of the tolerance. Performance remains acceptable, but SP is expected to update groundspeed before each turn so the lead point stays accurate.

texts_at.0: SP turned onto the arc with the IP computing the turn radius from groundspeed and talking through the conversion to NM per minute. This is SP's first exposure to computing a turn radius from groundspeed rather than indicated airspeed, and the conversion has not yet become routine. The Training Section still expects IP assistance for this maneuver at this point. SP is expected to begin computing the turn radius independently from groundspeed, with the IP available to confirm the conversion.
texts_at.1: SP computed a turn radius from groundspeed to the standard expected at this stage, letting the arc error reach 2 DME, at the limit of the tolerance, before the correction was made. The correction followed the IP prompting a check of the DME rather than SP's own recheck of groundspeed. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to refresh groundspeed before each turn rather than carrying a stale figure forward.
texts_at.2: SP rechecked groundspeed without prompting, letting the arc error reach about 1.5 DME before recomputing the radius and closing back onto the arc. The groundspeed to NM per minute conversion is still subject to a small rounding error before the minus 2 rule is applied. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to carry the conversion to the same precision every time rather than rounding it early.
texts_at.3: SP computed the turn radius from the current groundspeed in NM per minute and used it as the lead point on most turns, rolling out on the arc within 1 DME with the value cross-checked against the DME behaviour. One turn needed a small correction after a slightly stale groundspeed figure, without leaving the standard. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus. SP is expected to refresh groundspeed for that turn as reliably as for the others.

texts_above.1: SP computed a turn radius from groundspeed, letting the arc error reach about 2.0 NM, at the +/-2 NM limit, before the correction was made. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. The result is above the code required for this Training Section at this stage of training.
texts_above.2: SP rechecked groundspeed without prompting, letting the arc error reach 1.5 NM before recomputing the radius and closing back inside 1 NM. Carrying the conversion to the same precision every time, rather than rounding it early, would remove that excursion. error_modes.label: ARC TO RADIAL LEAD POINT NOT CONVERTED INTO RADIALS (60 TO 1)

texts.0: SP, due to leaving the lead point in miles and never converting it into radials with the 60 divided by arc distance rule, started the turn off the 20 NM arc at the wrong radial. Instead of the six radials of lead that a 2 NM turn radius gives, the turn was begun practically on the course, and the aircraft went 3.0 NM through the arc before rolling out, exceeding the +/-2 NM limit. The IP directed the reintercept back to the arc.
texts.1: SP, due to using a fixed number of radials of lead irrespective of arc distance instead of the 60 divided by arc conversion, began the turn late and let the DME open to 2.0 NM, at the +/-2 NM limit. The IP had to call the radial before SP started back toward the arc, and the recovery was slow.
texts.2: SP, due to an inaccurate conversion of the lead point from miles into radials on the arc being flown, started the turn slightly late and reached 1.5 NM of arc error, between the +/-1 NM and +/-2 NM values. SP recomputed the radials per mile without prompting and returned inside 1 NM in good time.
texts.3: SP converted the lead point in miles into radials with the 60 divided by arc distance rule before each turn and kept the arc within +/-1 NM. The turns were begun at the computed radial and the DME required only minor adjustment afterwards.
texts.4: SP applied the 60 to 1 conversion accurately for the arc distance in use and started every turn at the computed radial, holding the DME within a few tenths of a mile. The relation between radials per mile and arc distance was used without hesitation.
texts.marginal: SP made the conversion into radials but used a value carried over from a different arc distance, so the lead was slightly optimistic and the arc error settled on the outer part of the band. The result stays within standards, but SP is expected to recompute the radials per mile for the actual arc rather than reuse a previous figure.

texts_at.0: SP turned off the arc with the IP computing the radials of lead for the arc distance being flown and talking through the conversion. The Training Section introduces this maneuver at this point and does not yet ask for an independent standard. SP is expected to begin converting the lead point into radials independently for each arc distance, with the IP available to confirm the value.
texts_at.1: SP converted the lead point into radials to the standard expected at this stage, letting the arc error open to 2 DME, at the tolerance limit, before the correction was made. error_modes.label: CDI RATE OF MOVEMENT NOT USED TO REFINE THE LEAD POINT

texts.0: SP, due to reading the CDI as pegged and ignoring its rate of movement, although at normal T-6 airspeeds it stays off the wall within 10 degrees of the desired course, did not refine the computed lead point during the intercept. The turn was flown on the raw calculation alone and the aircraft finished 2.8 NM off the arc, past the +/-2 NM limit, with no correction started. The IP assigned the heading needed to recover the arc.
texts.1: SP, due to not using the rate of CDI movement as the cue for the lead point, kept the initial computed value although the needle was already moving quickly, and the arc error reached 2.0 NM, at the +/-2 NM limit. The turn was adjusted only after the IP's verbal prompt to watch the CDI rate, and the arc was regained late.
texts.2: SP, due to a late reading of the CDI rate of movement during the intercept, refined the lead point only after the needle had moved appreciably and reached 1.5 NM of arc error, between the +/-1 NM and +/-2 NM values. SP made the adjustment without prompting and settled back inside 1 NM without IP input.
texts.3: SP used the rate of CDI movement to refine the computed lead point during the intercept and held the arc within +/-1 NM. The needle was kept in the cross-check with the DME, so the turn was started and stopped at the right points.
texts.4: SP read the CDI rate continuously and adjusted the lead point as the needle rate changed, so the arc was held within a few tenths of a mile. The refinement was made before any DME trend became measurable.
texts.marginal: SP did use the CDI rate but only as a confirmation after the turn had been started, rather than as the cue for refining the lead point, so each intercept finished on the outer part of the tolerance. Performance is acceptable, but SP is expected to read the needle rate early enough to correct the lead point before the turn is begun.

texts_at.0: SP flew the intercept with the IP reading the rate of CDI movement and talking through refining the lead point from it. error_modes.label: BANK ANGLE OTHER THAN 30 DEGREES NOT ACCOUNTED FOR IN THE LEAD POINT

texts.0: SP, due to flying the turn with about 15 degrees of bank while the lead point had been computed for 30 degrees, did not allow for the larger turn radius that less bank produces. The turn was started at the unadjusted lead point and the aircraft went 2.7 NM through the arc, beyond the +/-2 NM limit, without any correction. The IP had to take the heading assignment to re-establish the arc.
texts.1: SP, due to a shallow bank that was never matched by an increase of the computed lead point, overshot and let the arc error reach 2.0 NM, at the +/-2 NM limit. The turn was tightened only after the IP prompted for more bank, and the DME returned toward the nominal value slowly.
texts.2: SP, due to a bank angle noticeably below the 30 degrees on which the lead point was based, went slightly through the arc and reached 1.5 NM of error, between the +/-1 NM and +/-2 NM values. SP recognized the shallow bank without prompting, increased it and closed back inside 1 NM in good time.
texts.3: SP flew the turns at the 30 degrees of bank on which the lead point calculation is based and held the arc within +/-1 NM. Where less bank was used the lead point was increased accordingly, so no overshoot developed.
texts.4: SP matched bank angle and lead point exactly on every turn, adjusting the lead whenever less than 30 degrees of bank was used, and kept the arc within a few tenths of a mile. Bank was steady through each turn with no drift in the roll-out point.
texts.marginal: SP kept the arc inside tolerance but tended to roll into slightly less bank than the 30 degrees assumed by the calculation, then absorb the difference with a correction after roll-out. The result meets standards, but SP is expected to fly the planned bank or adjust the lead point for it, so the roll-out arrives on the arc rather than through it.

texts_at.0: SP flew the turn onto the arc with the IP calling the bank angle used and talking through the lead point it was computed for. SP is expected to begin matching bank angle and lead point independently, with the IP available to confirm the adjustment.
texts_at.1: SP accounted for bank angle in the lead point to the standard expected at this stage, letting the arc error reach 2 DME, at the maximum tolerance, before the turn was tightened. The correction followed the IP's prompt for more bank rather than SP's own recognition of the shallow bank. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to fly the planned 30 degrees of bank or adjust the lead point for a shallower turn before the arc is missed.
texts_at.2: SP recognized the shallow bank without prompting, letting the arc error reach about 1.5 DME before increasing bank and closing back inside the desired tolerance in good time. Bank is still noticeably below the 30 degrees the lead point is based on before the correction is made. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to fly the planned bank angle from the roll-in rather than correcting it partway through the turn.
texts_at.3: SP flew the turns at the 30 degrees of bank on which the lead point calculation is based and held the arc within 1 DME on most turns, increasing the lead point where less bank was used so no overshoot developed.
